cells.tense: You are letting what you see sit for a moment before you reach for the explanation.
cells.ask: Leave one clear read about someone you love unargued for a week, and notice what the quiet does.
cells.core:
You can tell what matters before you can say why, and you don't flinch from the not-knowing that follows. The read arrives before the argument does, and it tends to hold up. Here is what that looks like when it is going well: you notice something about a person or a room, you say it once, and you let it stand.

What you do next is what keeps it clean. You pass along what you see without needing to hold everything around it, and people near you can hear the difference between being told and being met. Setting down what no longer serves is making room for what comes next, and you do that quietly while you carry the day. Stay with the pen.
cells.sheetLine: You see what matters before you can say why.
cells.place: the practice of setting down what no longer serves

cells.tense: You are storing every piece against a future where you might need it, and the future keeps moving further out.
cells.ask: Give one thing away — a note, a book, a folder you haven't opened — and watch what the empty shelf does.
cells.core:
You are pushing to have it all. Every piece gets kept, cross-checked, held against a moment that hasn't arrived. Looking has become a search for more looking, and the wall is made of everything you couldn't stop adding. The next step hides behind the pile.

A better system won't help. A smaller one will. Put one piece down where you can see it, then pick the next. Some of what you carry was handed to you, and your grip has made it heavier than it needed to be. What is left after that is what actually needs tending, and you will know it the moment it stands alone.
cells.sheetLine: You are holding everything against a future that hasn't come.
cells.place: the practice of setting down what no longer serves

cells.tense: You knew what to look at once, and you have been standing at a door that is already behind you.
cells.ask: Name one thing you keep checking with other people. Say it plainly to someone, with no question mark at the end.
cells.core:
Something in you knows, and has known, and you keep handing the question out anyway. You ask the room whether it agrees, and the answers settle nothing because they weren't the point. Here is this when it is going well: you feel the read land, you stay with it a beat, and you move. You don't need the whole road lit, only the next few steps.

What you can lean on is the part of you that has been right before, in small ways you didn't stop to count. Start there. Say what you see to one person and let them take it or leave it. The asking is not the problem; the asking instead of looking is. Pick the next step you can actually see, and take it.
cells.sheetLine: You know it. You keep asking the room instead.
cells.place: the practice of setting down what no longer serves

cells.tense: Reads keep arriving that surprise you, and you file them under luck or instinct.
cells.ask: Keep a small log for a week: one line each time a call turns out right. Read it back and call it yours.
cells.core:
You are already steering with this. The decisions you call random keep landing well, and people come to you for reads you didn't notice you made. It is doing its work in the same moments you credit to chance. The pen is moving while your hand says it isn't.

Nothing here asks you to be more certain. It asks you to stop calling your own read a stranger. Notice one moment today where you saw something before the evidence arrived, and let that count as yours. The rest follows from the same honesty. What you already do, you can begin to own.
cells.sheetLine: You keep calling your own read an accident.
